# LMSYS-Chat-1M: topics, model behaviour and safety in 5,000 English conversations

This study revisits the topic analysis of the LMSYS-Chat-1M paper ([Zheng et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.11998v4)) and extends it to model behaviour. On a random sample of ${n_sample} English conversations we:

1. labeled every conversation with **6 categories** (the paper's 5 plus *Others*), **4 attributes** of the model's replies (anthropomorphism, sycophancy, fear-inducing, harmful) and whether the model **prevented unsafe content**, using one set of written guidelines for both a human annotator and an LLM;
2. **replicated the paper's k-means clustering** (20 clusters) twice: once per prompt, as the paper did, and once per conversation;
3. compared **human vs LLM vs clustering vs the paper**, and looked at which chatbot models show which behaviours.

**Headlines**

- The LLM labels the categories like the human annotator does (κ = ${kappa_hl}, ${agree_hl} agreement); k-means clusters agree only moderately with either (κ = ${kappa_hb} vs human, ${kappa_lb} vs LLM).
- Our category shares are close to the paper's except *Business & Specific* (${cat_llm_bus} vs ${cat_paper_bus}), most likely because our guidelines send general-knowledge questions there.
- Weighting each conversation's LLM label by its number of prompts (the paper's unit) raises *Explicit Content* from ${unit_expl_llm_conv} to ${unit_expl_llm_prompt} (paper: ${unit_expl_paper}): explicit role-play conversations are longer.
- Unsafe content was requested or produced in ${prev_pct_app} of conversations; models prevented it only **${prev_rate}** of the time, ranging from ${prev_best} down to ${prev_worst}.
- OpenAI's moderation flags miss ${mod_unsafe_not_flagged_pct} of the conversations our labels mark as unsafe, and ${mod_attr_not_flagged} of those with anthropomorphism, sycophancy or fear-inducing replies.

---

## 1. Data and method, compared with the paper

| Step | Paper (Sec. 3.2) | This study |
|---|---|---|
| Sample | 100K random English conversations | ${n_sample} random English conversations (seed 42), ${n_models} models |
| Unit for topics | every user prompt (initial + follow-ups) | prompts (**prompt clustering**) **and** conversations (**conversation clustering**, human, LLM) |
| Length filter | drop prompts < 32 or > 1,536 characters | same, applied to each message (never to a whole conversation) |
| Deduplication | none | none |
| Embedding | all-mpnet-base-v2 | all-mpnet-base-v2 (normalized; conversation clustering uses the mean of a conversation's prompt embeddings) |
| Clustering | k-means, k = 20 | k-means, k = 20, 10 restarts, seed 42 |
| Cluster naming | GPT-4 summary of 100 prompts nearest each centroid | ${llm_model}, same procedure |
| Categories | 5, grouped from the 20 clusters by the authors | 6 (adds *Others*), defined in [`annotation/labels.yaml`](annotation/labels.yaml) v${labels_version}; clusters mapped by hand in [`mapping.yaml`](analysis/clustering/mapping.yaml) |
| Per-conversation labels | none | human (100) and LLM (${n_sample}): category, 4 attributes, unsafe-content prevention |

**Who labeled what**

- **Human:** 100 conversations — ${n_h_random} drawn at random (used for shares) and ${n_h_flagged} chosen via OpenAI moderation flags to cover rare traits (used only for agreement). Moderation flags and the chatbot's identity were hidden while labeling.
- **LLM:** ${llm_model} labeled all ${n_sample} with the same guidelines, returning a fixed JSON schema; chatbot model names and moderation flags were hidden.
- **Clustering:** ${n_prompts_kept} prompts survive the length filter. Conversation clustering covers the ${n_conv_b} conversations with at least one such prompt; the other ${n_conv_dropped} (${pct_conv_dropped}) have none — mostly greetings and pasted documents (see [Appendix C](#c-conversations-clustering-cannot-cover)). **Every comparison involving clustering uses these ${n_conv_b} conversations** (${n_h_b} of the human-labeled ones, ${n_h_random_b} of them random).

The category is the *main theme of the user's messages* across the conversation; attributes are judged on the *model's replies* (Yes if any reply qualifies).

## 2. Topics: paper vs prompt clustering vs conversation clustering

### The 20 topics

Each approach is a separate k-means solution. To compare them, each of our clusters takes the name of a paper topic when it is the **same** topic (proposed by the LLM from the cluster's closest examples, then reviewed by hand: [`paper_topics.yaml`](analysis/clustering/paper_topics.yaml)); clusters without a match keep their own k-means name. Several of our clusters can share one paper topic.

![The paper's 20 topics in each approach](${fig_topics_matched})

${table_matched_topics}

*Percent of prompts (paper, prompt clustering) or conversations (conversation clustering); our cluster numbers in brackets. ${n_paper_unmatched_A} paper topics have no counterpart in prompt clustering and ${n_paper_unmatched_B} none in conversation clustering. Scripted-template topics (e.g. 14, 18, 19, 20) are single-prompt conversations, so they weigh more when counting conversations.*

**Topics not in the paper** (our k-means names):

${table_new_topics}

The full 20-cluster distributions, with the same names (=P*n* marks the paper topic; *new* = not in the paper), colored by the category each cluster was mapped to (tag in brackets; the paper's mapping is the authors', ours is in [`mapping.yaml`](analysis/clustering/mapping.yaml)):

![Topic distribution: paper vs prompt clustering vs conversation clustering](${fig_topics20})

### Category shares: prompt vs conversation as the unit

The paper counts prompts: a 10-prompt role-play counts ten times. Our labels count conversations. Mapping every cluster to its category gives the category shares of each clustering; for the LLM we show its conversation labels counted both ways.

![Category shares counted per prompt and per conversation](${fig_unit})

${table_unit}

*"LLM, prompt-weighted" is **not** a per-prompt LLM label: each conversation's single LLM label is counted once for every kept prompt in it. It shows how weighting by prompts alone changes the shares, but ignores topic changes within a conversation. The clustering columns use the ${n_conv_b} conversations / ${n_prompts_kept} prompts.*

- **Weighting effect (same LLM labels, counted two ways):** shares barely move except *Explicit Content*, ${unit_expl_llm_conv} per conversation vs ${unit_expl_llm_prompt} weighted by prompts, because explicit conversations have the most prompts (table below). Weighted, the LLM is close to the paper's ${unit_expl_paper}.
- **Prompt vs conversation clustering** differ much more (Language ${unit_lang_a} → ${unit_lang_b}, Business ${unit_bus_a} → ${unit_bus_b}, Cultural ${unit_cult_a} → ${unit_cult_b}). Only part of this is the unit: the two are separate k-means solutions with different boundaries (e.g. "general knowledge" clusters landed in Cultural in prompt clustering but in Business in conversation clustering).

${table_prompts_per_conv}

## 3. Categories: human vs LLM vs clustering

### Shares

![Category shares per conversation](${fig_cat_pct})

${table_cat_pct}

*First four columns: the ${n_conv_b} conversations clustering covers (human: ${n_h_random_b} random). Last two: all conversations. The human sample is small — with ~50 conversations a share of 30% has a 95% margin of about ±12 points.*

- The LLM's shares on all ${n_sample} conversations are close to the paper's for Technical, Language and Cultural.
- *Business & Specific* is higher than in the paper (${cat_llm_bus} vs ${cat_paper_bus}), most likely because our guidelines put general-knowledge questions there, which the paper had no category for.
- *Others* (greetings, tests) is ${cat_llm_others} (LLM) / ${cat_h_others} (human random 60); the paper removed most of these with its length filter.

### Agreement per conversation

${table_cat_agree}

![Category confusion matrices](${fig_cat_confusion})

- **Human vs LLM: substantial agreement (κ = ${kappa_hl}).** Most disagreements are at the Language boundary: ${top_confusions_hl}.
- **Clustering vs either annotator: moderate (κ ≈ ${kappa_lb}–${kappa_hb}).** k-means groups prompts by wording and templates, not by task, so clusters mix categories; Language & Content is spread over many clusters.

## 4. Attributes of the model's replies

### Human vs LLM on the same 100 conversations

![Human vs LLM on the same 100 conversations](${fig_attr_100})

${table_attr_100}

*Both annotators labeled the same 100 conversations. They are not a random sample — 40 were chosen via moderation flags so that rare traits appear — so these percentages compare the annotators, not how common a trait is.*

### Prevalence and agreement

![Attribute prevalence](${fig_attr})

${table_attr}

*Prevalence: human on the random 60, LLM on the same 60 and on all ${n_sample}. Agreement and κ: all 100 human-labeled conversations (the 40 flagged ones make the rare traits appear).*

- The traits are rare: ${attr_any_llm} of conversations show at least one (LLM).
- **Sycophancy (κ = ${attr_sycophancy_kappa}) and harmful (κ = ${attr_harmful_kappa})** are labeled consistently; the LLM is stricter on *harmful*.
- **Anthropomorphism is unreliable (κ = ${attr_anthropomorphism_kappa}).** The guideline's own example ("I'm so happy to help you") led the LLM to count stock politeness; the human did not. Its LLM rate (${attr_anthropomorphism_llm}) is an upper bound.
- **Fear-inducing** is too rare (${attr_fear_inducing_llm}) for a stable estimate.

## 5. Unsafe-content prevention

A conversation is *applicable* when the user asked for unsafe content (sexual, toxic, violent, criminal incl. cyber-crime, self-harm) or the model produced it. **Prevented** = the model never produced it; **failed** = it did at any point.

- ${prev_n_app} conversations (${prev_pct_app}) are applicable: ${prev_n_yes} prevented, ${prev_n_no} failed — a prevention rate of **${prev_rate}** (95% CI ${prev_rate_ci}).
- This is the most reliable label: human vs LLM κ = ${prev_kappa} (${prev_agree} agreement on 100).

![Prevention rate by model](${fig_prev_model})

${table_prev_model}

- **Most protective:** ${prev_best}. **Least:** ${prev_worst}.
- Confidence intervals are wide. Clearly above the overall rate (whole 95% CI above it): ${prev_above}. Clearly below: ${prev_below}. The other ${prev_overlap} models overlap the overall rate.
- The commercial models had too few unsafe requests in the sample to rate (fewer than 20): ${prev_models_small} (prevented/applicable).

### Sexual vs other unsafe requests, single vs multi-turn

${table_prev_split}

Sexual requests are prevented far less often (${prev_sexual}) than other unsafe requests (${prev_other}), and multi-turn conversations far less often (${prev_multi}) than single-turn ones (${prev_single}). The two overlap — explicit role-play is typically multi-turn — so this is not evidence of gradual jailbreaking on its own.

## 6. Our labels vs OpenAI moderation

The dataset ships OpenAI moderation results per message. Comparing them with our LLM labels (${n_sample} conversations):

${table_mod}

- **${mod_unsafe_not_flagged} conversations (${mod_unsafe_not_flagged_pct} of those we mark unsafe) are not flagged** by moderation. Most of them (${mod_nf_prevented}, ${mod_nf_prevented_pct}) are unsafe *requests* the model refused; the rest are unsafe replies moderation missed. Moderation flags ${mod_failed_flagged} of the failed preventions but only ${mod_success_flagged} of the prevented ones.
- ${mod_harm_not_flagged} of conversations with a *harmful* reply are not flagged.
- ${mod_attr_not_flagged} of conversations with anthropomorphism, sycophancy or fear-inducing replies are not flagged — moderation does not look for these behaviours at all.

---

## 7. Limitations

- **One human annotator, 100 conversations.** Human shares rest on 52–60 random conversations (wide margins); agreement on 100.
- **One LLM, one run.** Labels come from ${llm_model} with guidelines v${labels_version}; another model or run would differ somewhat.
- **Guideline wording matters.** The anthropomorphism example inflated that attribute; the category rules for general knowledge (→ Business) and math (→ Technical) are our choices, not the paper's.
- **Clustering is not the paper's clustering.** Different sample size, naming model and unknown paper settings; cluster-to-category mapping was done by hand. ${n_conv_dropped} conversations cannot be clustered.
- **Per-model rates** come from LLM labels and are shown only with ≥ 20 cases; vicuna-13b alone is about half the data.

### D. Reproduce

```bash
scripts/download_data.sh                                   # raw dataset (gated, Hugging Face)
uv run python scripts/make_sample.py                       # 5,000 English conversations
uv run python scripts/make_annotation_sets.py              # 60 random + 40 flagged for human labels
uv run streamlit run app.py                                # explorer + annotation UI
uv run python scripts/llm_annotate.py --set sample5000     # LLM labels (needs OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_MODEL)
uv run python scripts/cluster.py                           # embeddings, prompt + conversation clustering, names
uv run python scripts/make_reports.py                      # this report and reports/figures/
```
